subject: business
title: Porter's Five Forces: why some industries are more profitable than others
dek: In 1979 Michael Porter argued in Harvard Business Review that an industry's profits are set by five competitive forces, not just by rivalry. This lesson explains each force, then looks at why airlines have struggled for a century and how Southwest built a strategy that fit the structure.
honesty: This lesson explains the framework as Porter described it in his 1979 and 2008 Harvard Business Review articles and on Harvard Business School's Institute for Strategy and Competitiveness site. The Warren Buffett quotation comes from his 2007 Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letter. The Southwest Airlines discussion follows Porter's 1996 article 'What Is Strategy?'. The application to streaming is our own illustration, not Porter's. The lesson contains no images and deliberately avoids industry profit figures we could not check against a primary source.

timeline.label: 'How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy' in HBR
timeline.detail: Michael Porter, a young Harvard Business School professor trained in industrial organization economics, publishes the article that introduces the five forces.

timeline.label: Competitive Strategy
timeline.detail: Porter expands the idea into the book Competitive Strategy: Techniques for Analyzing Industries and Competitors.

timeline.label: Competitive Advantage
timeline.detail: Porter's next book introduces the value chain, which looks at how a single company's activities create cost or differentiation advantages.

timeline.label: 'What Is Strategy?'
timeline.detail: Porter argues in HBR that operational effectiveness is not strategy, and uses Southwest Airlines to show how a set of activities that fit together creates a defensible position.

timeline.label: 'The Five Competitive Forces That Shape Strategy'
timeline.detail: Porter republishes and updates the framework in HBR, adding guidance on common mistakes such as treating industry growth rate or government as a sixth force.

fun_fact.title: A capitalist at Kitty Hawk
fun_fact.text: In his 2007 shareholder letter, Warren Buffett wrote that in airlines 'a durable competitive advantage has proven elusive ever since the days of the Wright Brothers,' and that a farsighted capitalist present at Kitty Hawk 'would have done his successors a huge favor by shooting Orville down.' Buffett was joking, but the joke is a fair one-line summary of what a five forces analysis of airlines tends to show.

glossary.explain: Harvard Business School professor, born in 1947, whose work on industry structure, competitive advantage and the value chain shaped the modern strategy field.

Porter's framework of five pressures that together set an industry's profit potential: rivalry among existing competitors, the threat of new entrants, the bargaining power of suppliers, the bargaining power of buyers, and the threat of substitutes.
The underlying economic characteristics of an industry, as captured by the five forces, which determine how the value it creates is divided among companies, customers, suppliers and potential rivals.

Competition between current players through price cuts, new products, advertising and service. Porter notes that price competition is the most damaging kind because it transfers profit straight to customers.
The pressure that possible newcomers put on prices and investment. It depends on barriers to entry and on how strongly incumbents are expected to retaliate.
Advantages incumbents hold over newcomers, such as economies of scale, network effects, customer switching costs, capital requirements, access to distribution, and government policy.
The ability of the companies that sell inputs to an industry to capture value by charging more, limiting quality or shifting costs onto the industry.
The ability of customers to force prices down or demand more, which is greatest when buyers are large, products are undifferentiated and switching is cheap.
Pressure from products that meet the same need in a different way, such as videoconferencing as a substitute for business travel. Substitutes cap the price an industry can charge.
Porter's 1985 concept describing the separate activities a company performs to design, produce, sell and support its product, each a possible source of cost or differentiation advantage.
Performing similar activities better than rivals. Porter argues in 'What Is Strategy?' that this is necessary but not a strategy, because good practices are easily copied.
In Porter's 1996 article, the way a company's activities reinforce one another, making the whole system much harder to imitate than any single activity.
Porter's 1980 book that expanded the five forces into a full method for analysing industries and competitors.
Porter's original 1979 Harvard Business Review article introducing the five forces.
Porter's 1996 Harvard Business Review article distinguishing strategy from operational effectiveness, with Southwest Airlines as a central example.

A US airline that Porter used as his main example of a strategy built from a tightly fitting set of activities: short point-to-point routes, one aircraft type, quick gate turnarounds and no meals or interline baggage transfer.
Chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, whose annual shareholder letters are widely read for their plain-spoken views on business economics.
Hamilton Helmer's framework of seven conditions that let a single company earn persistent above-normal returns. It is covered in an earlier Saturday lesson and works well alongside the five forces.

sections.title: The question: why do some industries make more money than others?

blocks.text: In the 1970s, most companies thought about competition narrowly. They watched their direct rivals, tracked market share and tried to win on price or features. Economists who studied industrial organization had a broader view: they measured how concentrated an industry was and linked that to profitability, but their work was written for antitrust regulators, not for managers who wanted to earn more.

Michael Porter was trained in that economics tradition at Harvard and taught at Harvard Business School. In his 1979 Harvard Business Review article 'How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy', he turned the economists' tools around. Instead of asking how to keep industries competitive for the public good, he asked a manager's question: what determines how much profit an industry can earn, and where in that industry can one company find a position that protects it?

His answer was that rivalry with direct competitors is only one of five forces. Customers, suppliers, possible newcomers and substitute products all compete for the value an industry creates. When these forces are strong, as in airlines, almost no company earns attractive returns for long. When they are weak, as Porter suggested for industries such as software or soft drinks in his 2008 update, many companies in the industry can be profitable.
The framework spread quickly. Porter's 1980 book Competitive Strategy became a standard text in MBA programmes, and the five forces became one of the most widely taught tools in business education.

sections.title: The five forces, one at a time

blocks.text: The first force is rivalry among existing competitors. Rivalry reduces profits most when competitors are numerous or similar in size, when industry growth is slow, when exit barriers are high, and when competitors compete on price. Porter stresses that price competition is the most harmful form, because it hands profits directly to customers. Competition on features, service or brand can instead expand the value an industry creates.

The second force is the threat of new entrants. A company does not need actual new competitors to feel this force; the possibility of entry alone keeps prices down. The threat depends on barriers to entry: economies of scale on the supply side, network effects on the demand side, the cost to customers of switching, the capital required, incumbents' access to distribution channels, and government policy such as licences.

The third force is the bargaining power of suppliers. Suppliers are powerful when they are more concentrated than the industry they sell to, when their product is differentiated or essential, when switching to another supplier is costly, or when they could credibly enter the industry themselves. Porter's examples include labour unions with strong bargaining positions and suppliers of key components with few alternatives.

The fourth force is the bargaining power of buyers. Customers are powerful when there are few of them or each buys in large volumes, when the product is standardised, when switching is cheap, and when the purchase is a large share of their own costs, which makes them shop hard on price. Buyers can be companies, such as large retailers buying from manufacturers, or individual consumers.

The fifth force is the threat of substitutes. A substitute meets the same need through a different kind of product. Porter's examples include videoconferencing as a substitute for business travel and plastic as a substitute for aluminium. Substitutes are easy to overlook because they look so different from the industry's own product, but they place a ceiling on prices.

items: Rivalry: how fiercely current competitors fight, especially on price.
New entrants: how easily a newcomer could join and add capacity.
Suppliers: how much value input sellers can capture.
Buyers: how much value customers can capture.
Substitutes: how easily customers can meet the same need another way.

blocks.text: In the 2008 article Porter also warns against common mistakes. Industry growth rate, technology and government are not forces in their own right; they matter only through their effect on the five. A fast-growing industry is not automatically attractive if growth draws in entrants or if suppliers are powerful. And the purpose of the analysis is not to label an industry as good or bad, but to understand why profitability is what it is, and then to find a position where the forces are weakest or to reshape them in the company's favour.

sections.title: Airlines, and how Southwest found a position within them

blocks.text: Airlines are the classic example of an industry where all five forces are strong. Rivalry is intense because carriers offer a largely similar product, flying the same routes at published prices, and because an empty seat earns nothing once the plane departs, so there is constant pressure to cut fares. Suppliers are concentrated: a few manufacturers build large passenger jets, and pilots and other workers are often represented by strong unions. Buyers can compare fares across airlines in seconds, and many treat flying as a commodity purchase. Substitutes such as cars, trains and videoconferencing limit what airlines can charge on many trips.

Warren Buffett described the result in his 2007 letter to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders. He called airlines an example of the worst kind of business, one that 'grows rapidly, requires significant capital to engender the growth, and then earns little or no money.' He added that 'a durable competitive advantage has proven elusive ever since the days of the Wright Brothers.'

Yet Porter's 1996 article 'What Is Strategy?' uses an airline as its main example of good strategy. Southwest Airlines did not try to beat the full-service carriers at their own game. It chose to serve price-sensitive travellers on short point-to-point routes between mid-sized cities and secondary airports, and it designed every activity around that choice. Porter lists the elements: no meals, no assigned seats, no interline baggage checking, no premium classes, a fleet of a single aircraft type (the Boeing 737), and very fast turnarounds at the gate that let each plane fly more trips per day.

Porter's point is that each of these activities supports the others. One aircraft type makes maintenance and crew training cheaper and turnarounds faster. Skipping meals and baggage transfers also speeds turnarounds. Frequent departures make the service attractive enough to compete with driving. A rival that copied one feature, such as cheaper fares, would gain little without the whole system. Porter called this fit, and he argued it is what makes a position hard to imitate.

He also describes what happened when a rival tried. Continental Airlines launched a low-fare operation called Continental Lite that copied some of Southwest's practices while keeping parts of its full-service model, such as travel agent commissions and its frequent-flier programme. Porter writes that the attempt produced delays, congestion, and large operating losses, and that Continental eventually gave up. Trying to straddle both positions meant it got the benefits of neither.

Read together, the two articles show how the frameworks connect. The five forces explain why the airline industry as a whole earns low returns. The positioning argument in 'What Is Strategy?' explains how one company can still choose a set of customers and activities where those forces press on it less, by making itself a cheaper alternative to driving and by keeping its costs below those of rivals who serve everyone.

As a brief illustration of our own, not Porter's, the same lens helps explain debates about video streaming in the 2020s. Barriers to entry fell as many media companies launched services, rivalry rose, owners of popular shows gained supplier power, and subscribers could cancel and switch with a few clicks. A five forces reading suggests why many services have struggled to earn the margins investors once expected, even while the industry kept growing.

sections.title: Try it on your own industry

blocks.text: Pick an industry you know well. For each of the five forces, write one sentence on whether it is strong or weak and why. Then ask which force most limits profits, and whether any company in that industry has found a position, like Southwest's, where that force presses on it less. If you read the Seven Powers lesson, ask a second question: does that company also hold one of Helmer's Powers that would stop rivals from copying its position?
